1.title: Governing Generative & Agentic AI
1.text: Everything so far gives you a solid governance toolkit. But generative AI, and now agentic AI, strain that toolkit in new ways. This module is about the frontier — the systems that create, and the systems that act — and the extra controls they demand.

1.title: Why Generative AI Breaks Classic Governance
1.text: Let's be precise about why generative AI is harder to govern. Compare it to classic, predictive AI. Predictive AI gives bounded outputs — a category, a score — that you can test against a known right answer. It usually runs internally, it's relatively stable. Generative AI is the opposite on every count. Its outputs are open-ended — it can produce any text or image. There's often no single right answer to test against. It's put directly into users' hands. And it's updated constantly by the vendor underneath you. Most of our classic controls quietly assumed a model that predicts. Generative models create — and that fundamentally changes the shape of the risk. The earlier controls still apply, but they need new additions, which is what this module adds.

1.title: Hallucination
1.text: First and most famous: hallucination. A generative model will produce confident, fluent, completely fabricated information — including fake citations to sources that don't exist. And here's the uncomfortable truth: you cannot fully eliminate this, because the model is fundamentally optimizing for plausible, not for true. So you don't govern the behavior away — you govern the use around it. Ground the model in trusted sources using retrieval, so it answers from real documents. Require citations and verify them. Constrain its scope. Insert human review for any high-stakes use. And set user expectations honestly. The governance mindset shift is important: when you can't fix the model, you bound the use.

1.title: IP & Copyright — Inputs and Outputs
1.text: Intellectual property, which we flagged back in Module 2, is acute for generative AI, and it cuts both ways. On the input side: was the model trained on copyrighted or licensed material without permission? There's active litigation on exactly this question all over the world right now. On the output side: could something the model generates infringe someone else's copyright — and separately, who even owns AI-generated output, and can you copyright it at all? The honest answer is that the law is genuinely unsettled. So you manage the exposure contractually and operationally: get indemnification from your vendors, track provenance, filter outputs for known infringement, and set clear usage policies for your staff. You manage the risk while the courts catch up.

1.title: Data Leakage & Prompt Injection
1.text: Two security risks deserve special attention with generative AI, because they're new doors. The first is leakage out: employees paste confidential information or personal data into a public chatbot, and that data may be logged or even used to train the vendor's model. Your trade secret just left the building through a text box. The second is injection in: malicious text hidden in a document, an email, or a webpage hijacks the model's instructions and makes it do something it shouldn't. To close the first door: enterprise tooling with explicit no-training guarantees, and data-loss-prevention scanning on prompts. To close the second: input and output filtering, least privilege for any tools the model can use, and a simple rule — treat all retrieved content as untrusted. Two doors: data walking out, and instructions sneaking in. Lock both.

1.title: Deepfakes & Content Provenance
1.text: As synthetic media gets indistinguishable from the real thing, a whole field of provenance tooling is emerging to answer one question: where did this content come from? Watermarking embeds a hidden signal into AI-generated output. Standards like C2PA — Content Credentials — attach a cryptographic record of how a piece of content was made, like a tamper-evident nutrition label. Detection tools exist, but they're imperfect and locked in an arms race with the generators. And disclosure — simply labeling AI-generated content — is now legally required in a growing number of places. The big-picture takeaway: content provenance is becoming core trust infrastructure, because detection alone is a losing battle. Proving authenticity beats trying to spot fakes.

1.title: Foundation-Model Governance
1.text: How do you govern a foundation model you didn't train and can't see inside? You focus on the two things you actually control. Picture the stack: the model provider governs the training, the safety evaluations, and any systemic risk. End users sit at the bottom. And you're in the middle — so you govern your selection of the model, and how you wrap it. Selection: choose based on capabilities, published safety evaluations, transparency like model cards, the data terms, certifications, and the update policy. Wrapping: the configuration, the guardrails you add, and — critically — what data you allow to flow to it. You can't govern the model's internals, so you govern your choice of model and everything you build around it.

1.title: Enterprise GenAI Rollout & Shadow AI
1.text: When an organization rolls generative AI out to its workforce, the governance challenge is mostly about shadow AI — and the solution is counterintuitive. Your instinct might be to ban it. But ban it, and people just use it on their personal devices, completely ungoverned. The winning play is to make the safe path the easy path. Provide approved enterprise tools with no-training guarantees, logging, and controls. Write an acceptable-use policy people will actually read. Use role-based access. Invest in training and AI literacy. And create an easy intake path for new use cases. As your governed options get better and easier, that shadow-AI iceberg from Module 7 starts to shrink — because the official route is now genuinely more convenient than going rogue.

1.title: Agentic AI — The Autonomy Leap
1.text: Now the frontier of the frontier: agentic AI. Think of a ladder of autonomy. At the bottom, the AI just suggests, and a human decides. One rung up, it acts but needs approval first. Higher, it acts and then reports. At the top, it acts autonomously within set bounds. As you climb that ladder, the governance stakes climb with you. Because here's the leap: generative AI produces words. Agentic AI takes actions — it books, it buys, it sends, it changes records, it calls real APIs in the real world. A hallucinated sentence is embarrassing. A hallucinated action — a wrong purchase, a wrong email to a customer, a wrong database change — has consequences. As autonomy rises, the blast radius of a mistake grows.

1.title: The Agentic Oversight Problem
1.text: So governing agents requires a new set of controls, because oversight shifts from reviewing outputs to bounding actions. What does that look like? Scoped permissions and least privilege — what tools and systems is this agent even allowed to touch? Human-in-the-loop checkpoints for consequential actions — the agent must pause and ask before it does something irreversible or expensive. Hard spending and action limits. Full logging and traceability of every action it takes, so you can reconstruct what happened. A kill switch to stop it. And testing in sandboxes before it touches anything real. Be aware: as of 2026, standards bodies are actively writing agentic-specific controls, and this is the single fastest-moving area in all of AI governance. Expect what you know here to evolve quickly.

1.title: Helios Governs Its GenAI Assistant
1.text: Let's bring Helios's second AI system — the customer-facing generative assistant — under control. Helios uses an enterprise language model with a contract guaranteeing its data won't be used for training. It grounds the assistant using retrieval over its own verified help-center content, which sharply cuts hallucination. It puts up a clear "you're chatting with an AI" disclosure. It runs data-loss-prevention and output filters. It locks the assistant's scope to support topics, with escalation to a human when needed. It monitors for harmful or biased outputs. And notice the last, deliberate choice: Helios does not give this assistant autonomous power to change customer accounts — not yet. It withholds agency until it can bound it safely. Knowing what not to automate yet is itself a mature governance decision.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: To recap the frontier. Generative AI breaks classic controls through hallucination, IP issues, data leakage, prompt injection, and deepfakes — and the move is to govern the use and manage the exposure, since you can't fix the model. For foundation models, you govern your selection and your wrapping. For enterprise rollout, make the safe path the easy path. And agentic AI shifts oversight from reviewing outputs to bounding actions — least privilege, human checkpoints, hard limits, traceability, and a kill switch. Remember, this is the fastest-changing area in the field. Finally, in Module 11, the last piece — proving your governance actually works, and where your career goes from here.
